new_entities.name: CPAP for severe obstructive sleep apnea
aliases: continuous positive airway pressure for severe OSA
CPAP in severe obstructive sleep apnea
new_entities.description: Continuous positive airway pressure treatment used in adults with severe or at least moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea.

new_entities.name: Resistant hypertension
new_entities.description: Persistent hypertension despite a multidrug antihypertensive regimen, often including a diuretic, or hypertension requiring multiple drugs to achieve control.

edges.effect_quant: In resistant hypertension with severe or moderate-severe OSA, HIPARCO lowered 24-hour mean blood pressure by 3.1 mmHg versus control, while smaller cohorts showed larger pre-post systolic reductions after CPAP initiation.
edges.population: adults with severe or at least moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and resistant or refractory hypertension
edges.mechanism: CPAP may reduce sympathetic overactivity, nocturnal hypoxemia, and nondipping blood-pressure patterns that amplify multidrug-resistant hypertension in OSA.
edges.summary: Among OSA phenotypes, resistant hypertension is one of the clearest blood-pressure-responsive groups for CPAP. The effect is still modest on average, but it is more consistent than the hard cardiovascular event data.
edges.caveats: Some supportive studies are small or uncontrolled, and adherence matters strongly. The best evidence is for ambulatory blood-pressure lowering, not for long-term stroke or myocardial infarction prevention.

evidence.notes: Effect of CPAP on blood pressure in patients with obstructive sleep apnea and resistant hypertension: the HIPARCO randomized clinical trial.

effect_quant.comparator: 24-hour mean blood pressure with CPAP versus no CPAP in HIPARCO
